title: Fibre types: slow, fast and faster
goal: Tell type I, IIa and IIx fibres apart by their myosin, speed, power, fatigue resistance and oxidative capacity, compare endurance and sprint muscles, and judge what a muscle biopsy can and can't tell you.

steps.title: Three types, named by their myosin
steps.text:
Not all [myosin](g:myosin) is the same. Its big motor part, the [myosin heavy chain](g:myosin-heavy-chain) (MHC), comes in several isoforms (versions of one protein), and the isoform a fibre makes is the standard way to name its type [[c:ft-mhc-marker]].

Human limb muscles have three main types [[c:ft-three-types]]:

- [type I](g:type-i-fibre) (MHC I), slow-twitch;
- [type IIa](g:type-iia-fibre) (MHC IIa), fast;
- [type IIx](g:type-iix-fibre) (MHC IIx), the fastest. Older papers call it IIb.

All the fibres of one [motor unit](g:motor-unit) share a type, as you saw in the nervous system module.

The boxes are not watertight. Many fibres are [hybrids](g:hybrid-fibre) that make two or three MHC isoforms at once (I/IIa, IIa/IIx, I/IIa/IIx), and they can be a big share of the total [[c:ft-hybrids]].

claims.text: Myosin heavy chain isoforms are the standard marker of fibre type.

evidence.quote: Myosin heavy chain isoforms, whose complete inventory and expression pattern are now available, provide a useful marker for fiber types, both for the four major forms present in trunk and limb muscles and the minor forms present in head and neck muscles.

claims.text: Human limb muscle has three main fibre types: I, IIA and IIX (formerly called IIB).

evidence.quote: In this way the histological identification of three main human muscle fibre types (I, IIA and IIX, previously called IIB) has been followed by a precise description of molecular composition and functional and biochemical properties.

claims.text: Hybrid fibres that express more than one MHC isoform may be a significant share of all fibres.

evidence.quote: Hybrid fibers, which express more than one MHC type (I/IIa, IIa/IIx, I/IIa/IIx), may make up a significant proportion of fibers.

steps.title: Speed, power and staying power
steps.text:
The three types trade speed and power against endurance [[c:ft-fatigue]]:

| | type I | type IIa | type IIx |
|---|---|---|---|
| twitch speed | slow | fast | fastest |
| fatigue resistance | high | lower | low |
| oxidative capacity | high | fairly high | low |

In single fibres from biopsies, top shortening speed and peak power are lower in type I than in fast fibres, and IIa is slower than the fastest fast type [[c:ft-vmax]].

The gap in power is large. In single fibres from one champion hurdler, peak power per litre of fibre was about **35 W·L⁻¹ in IIx, 17 in IIa and 2.5 in type I** [[c:ft-power]]: IIx twice IIa and 14 times type I. That is one athlete, so take the exact ratios as a rough guide.

Fast fibres pay for that power: their cross-bridges cycle faster and burn ATP faster.

claims.text: Type I fibres are slow and fatigue resistant; type IIa are faster and less fatigue resistant; type IIx are fastest and highly fatigable.

evidence.quote: In humans, type I, or slow-twitch, fibers possess slower twitch speeds and are relatively fatigue resistant. Type IIa fibers, or fast oxidative glycolytic (FOG) fibers, present higher twitch speeds than type I fibers but are less fatigue resistant. Type IIx fibers, or fast glycolytic fibers, possess the fastest twitch speeds but are highly fatigable

claims.text: In human single fibres, maximum shortening velocity and peak power are lower in type I than in fast fibres, and lower in IIA than in the fastest fast fibres.

evidence.quote: All parameters were significantly lower in type I than in the fast (type IIA and IIB) fibres. Among fast fibres, Vmax, Wmax, Vopt and Vo were significantly lower in type IIA and than in IIB fibres, whereas Popt, Po/CSA and Vopt/Vmax were similar.

claims.text: In one champion sprinter, peak power was about 35 W·L⁻¹ in IIx fibres, 17 in IIa and 2.5 in type I.

evidence.quote: Power output of the MHC IIx fibers (35.1 ± 1.4 W/l) was 2-fold higher than MHC IIa fibers (17.1 ± 0.5 W/l) and 14-fold greater than MHC I fibers (2.5 ± 0.1 W/l).

steps.title: Endurance muscles and sprint muscles
steps.text:
Biopsies show how far athletes differ.

| who | muscle | fibres |
|---|---|---|
| elite distance runners | calf (gastrocnemius) | **79% slow-twitch** [[c:ft-runners]] |
| a world-champion hurdler | thigh (vastus lateralis) | **71% fast**, 24% pure IIx [[c:ft-sprinter]] |

Ordinary people spread widely too: about a quarter have under 35% or over 65% type I fibres in the thigh [[c:ft-spread]].

Pure IIx fibres are rare in most people. In biopsies from healthy, active young adults they made up only about 0.1% of fibres on average [[c:ft-iix-rare]]. A sprinter with 24% IIx is the exception.

So an endurance athlete's leg is mostly type I with a good share of IIa, and very little IIx. How much of that is talent and how much is training is the subject of the last lesson of this module.

claims.text: Elite distance runners' gastrocnemius had a high share (79%) of slow-twitch fibres.

evidence.quote: As previously demonstrated by others, the elite runners' muscles were characterized by a high percentage (79%) of slow twitch (ST) fibers.

claims.text: A world-class sprinter's vastus lateralis had 71% fast-twitch fibres, 24% of them pure IIx.

evidence.quote: The world-class sprinter's leg muscle had a high abundance (24%) of the pure MHC IIx muscle fibers with a total fast-twitch fiber population of 71%.

claims.text: About 25% of people have under 35% or over 65% type I fibres in the vastus lateralis.

evidence.quote: Skeletal muscle fiber type distribution is quite heterogeneous, with about 25% of North American Caucasian men and women having either less than 35% or more than 65% of type I fiber in their vastus lateralis muscle.

claims.text: In healthy, active young adults, pure type IIx fibres averaged about 0.1% of vastus lateralis fibres.

evidence.quote: Pure type IIX fibers and type IIX MyHC were randomly distributed and present in <24% of the analyzed samples, with the average content being 0.1% and 1.1%, respectively.

steps.title: How fibres are typed
steps.text:
Fibre types come from a [muscle biopsy](g:muscle-biopsy), usually of the vastus lateralis, typed in one of three ways [[c:ft-methods]]:

| method | what you get | blind spot |
|---|---|---|
| [SDS-PAGE](g:sds-page) of the whole sample | % of each MHC isoform in the piece | can't see hybrid fibres |
| staining thin slices | type of each fibre on a slide | hybrids hard to spot |
| SDS-PAGE of single fibres, one by one | each fibre's MHC mix, hybrids too | slow, few fibres |

Single-fibre typing is the best of the three, and the only one that also lets you test each fibre's force and speed.

A needle-free option exists: muscle carnosine measured by magnetic resonance rises with the share of type II fibres [[c:ft-carnosine]]. It was checked against biopsies in only 12 untrained men, so treat it as an estimate.

claims.text: Whole-sample (homogenate) electrophoresis gives the share of each MHC isoform but can't identify hybrid fibres; single-fibre typing is the best method.

evidence.quote: As a result, this technique lacks specificity in estimating the presence of hybrid fibers.

Single fiber typing is unequivocally the best method to delineate fiber type make-up from a biopsy specimen. Single fiber typing is also the only method that allows for mechanical and molecular analysis in a fiber type-specific fashion.

claims.text: Muscle carnosine measured by ¹H-MRS correlates with the area share of type II fibres.

evidence.quote: A significant positive correlation was found between muscle carnosine, measured by (1)H-MRS, and percentage area occupied by type II fibers.

steps.title: Reading fibre-type numbers with care
steps.text:
**One biopsy is a small window.** Fibre types are patchy within a muscle. Ten biopsies from the same thigh gave a within-person CV of 13–18% for fibre-type share [[c:ft-variability]]. To get the vastus lateralis within ±10 percentage points you need about three biopsies with at least 200 fibres counted [[c:ft-three-biopsies]].

**Links are not causes.** In 19 trained cyclists, those with more type I fibres were more efficient: r = 0.85 with delta efficiency [[c:ft-efficiency]]. A strong link, but a one-off measurement in one group of cyclists can't show that the fibres cause the efficiency, or rule out training history as a common cause.

So fibre-type figures are good for comparing groups, and weak for judging one athlete.

claims.text: Within-person coefficients of variation for fibre-type share across repeated vastus lateralis biopsies were 13–18%, so single biopsies are unreliable for fibre type.

evidence.quote: The average within-subject coefficient of variation for FT%, fCSA, fCSA%, and MyHC% ranged between 13% and 18% but was only 5% for fiber-specific myonuclear content, which reduced the variability for myonuclear domain size to 11%-12%.
However, single muscle biopsies should preferably not be used when studying fiber type- and fiber size-related aspects, given the notable sample-to-sample variability.

claims.text: Three biopsies with at least 200 fibres counted are needed to estimate vastus lateralis fibre type within ±10 percentage points.

evidence.quote: In conclusion, three biopsies with a minimum of 200 counted fibers are required to estimate the vastus lateralis fiber type composition within ±10 percentage points.

claims.text: In 19 trained cyclists, % type I fibres correlated with cycling efficiency (r = 0.85 with delta efficiency).

evidence.quote: The % Type I fibers was positively correlated with both DE (r = 0.85; P less than 0.001; N = 19) and GE (r = 0.75; P less than 0.001; N = 19) during cycling.

points: Fibre type is named by the myosin heavy chain: type I (slow), IIa (fast), IIx (fastest); hybrids make more than one.
Type I: slow, low power, oxidative and fatigue resistant. IIx: by far the most power per volume (14 times type I in one sprinter), but tires fast. IIa sits between.
Elite distance runners' calves were about 79% type I; a champion sprinter's thigh was 71% fast. Pure IIx is rare in most people.
Fibre type comes from biopsies: whole-sample SDS-PAGE misses hybrids, single-fibre typing is best, and one biopsy is noisy (CV 13–18%).

variants.stem: Human muscle fibres are classed as type I, IIa or IIx by which protein?

options.text: The isoform of myosin heavy chain they make
options.why: Right: MHC I, IIa and IIx define the three main types.

options.text: The isoform of actin they make
options.why: Skeletal muscle actin hardly differs between fibre types; myosin does.

options.text: The amount of myoglobin they hold
options.why: Myoglobin goes with oxidative capacity, but it isn't how types are defined.

options.text: The kind of troponin on their thin filaments
options.why: Troponin isoforms do differ, but the standard marker is the myosin heavy chain.

variants.stem: A lab reports that a cyclist's fibre is "type IIa". What has it measured to say so?

options.text: Which myosin heavy chain isoform the fibre contains
options.why: Right: type IIa means the fibre makes MHC IIa.

options.text: How many mitochondria the fibre contains
options.why: Mitochondrial content varies with training within each type; it doesn't define the type.

options.text: How thick the fibre is under the microscope
options.why: Fibre size changes with training and doesn't define the type.

options.text: How fast the fibre's nerve fires
options.why: Firing rate belongs to the motor neuron; the fibre type is set by its myosin.

options.text: A fibre that makes two or more MHC isoforms at once
options.why: Right: for example I/IIa or IIa/IIx.

options.text: A fibre supplied by two different motor neurons
options.why: Each adult fibre has one motor neuron; hybrid refers to its myosin.

options.text: A fibre made of type I and type II cells fused together
options.why: A fibre is one cell; a hybrid is one cell making a mix of myosins.

options.text: A fibre that switches type within one race
options.why: Type changes take weeks to months of training, not one race.

variants.stem: In a lab, a single fibre from a marathoner's calf shortens slowly, makes little power, and keeps its force over many minutes of repeated contractions. Which type is it most likely?

options.text: Type I
options.why: Right: slow, low power and fatigue resistant is the type I profile.

options.text: Type IIa
options.why: IIa fibres are faster and more powerful, and less fatigue resistant than type I.

options.text: Type IIx
options.why: IIx fibres are the fastest and tire quickly: the opposite profile.

options.text: A IIa/IIx hybrid
options.why: A IIa/IIx hybrid would be fast and fairly fatigable.

variants.stem: In the last 10 s of a criterium sprint, which fibre type gives the most power per volume of muscle, and what is its cost?

options.text: IIx: the most power, but it fatigues quickly
options.why: Right: IIx had about twice the power of IIa and 14 times type I, and is highly fatigable.

options.text: Type I: the most power, because it has the most mitochondria
options.why: Mitochondria set endurance, not peak power; type I has the lowest power.

options.text: IIa: the most power, and it never fatigues
options.why: IIa is powerful and fairly oxidative, but IIx has more power and no fibre is fatigue-free.

options.text: All three equal, since they share one cross-bridge cycle
options.why: The cycle is the same in kind, but its speed differs with the MHC isoform, so power differs greatly.

variants.stem: Biopsies of four athletes' calf muscles show 80%, 50%, 35% and 25% type I fibres. Which athlete is most likely the elite 10,000 m runner?

options.text: The one with 80% type I
options.why: Right: elite distance runners averaged about 79% slow-twitch fibres in the gastrocnemius.

options.text: The one with 50% type I
options.why: About half type I is typical of untrained people, not elite distance runners.

options.text: The one with 35% type I
options.why: A low type I share fits a sprint or power profile.

options.text: The one with 25% type I
options.why: This is a sprinter's profile: the champion hurdler had about 71% fast fibres.

variants.stem: A coach reads that a world-champion hurdler had 24% pure IIx fibres and concludes: "To sprint at world level you need about a quarter IIx fibres." What is the main weakness of this conclusion?

options.text: It rests on one athlete, who may be unusual even among sprinters
options.why: Right: a case study (n = 1) can describe one person, not set a requirement for a group.

options.text: IIx fibres don't exist in human muscle
options.why: Human muscle has MHC IIx fibres; they are just rare in most people.

options.text: Sprinting depends on type I fibres, not type II
options.why: Fast fibres matter more for sprinting; the issue is the sample size, not the direction.

options.text: Biopsies can't tell IIx from IIa fibres
options.why: Single-fibre SDS-PAGE separates MHC IIa from IIx; this study used it.

variants.stem: A study grinds up a whole biopsy from a triathlete's thigh and runs SDS-PAGE: 55% MHC I, 40% MHC IIa, 5% MHC IIx. What can't this result tell you?

options.text: How many fibres are hybrids rather than pure types
options.why: Right: a ground-up sample gives total isoform shares, so it can't say which fibres hold a mix.

options.text: Whether the sample contains any MHC IIx
options.why: It can: the IIx band is measured (5%).

options.text: The share of myosin that is the slow isoform
options.why: That is exactly what it reports: 55% MHC I.

options.text: Whether the sample was taken from muscle
options.why: Finding MHC isoforms at all shows it is muscle; this is no limit of the method.

variants.stem: A magnetic resonance scan shows a young runner's calf carnosine is well above the reference value. Without a biopsy, what is the best tentative reading?

options.text: A larger share of type II fibres, suggesting a sprint profile
options.why: Right: carnosine rises with the type II area share; explosive athletes had about 30% more than average.

options.text: A larger share of type I fibres, suggesting an endurance profile
options.why: The reverse: endurance athletes had about 20% less carnosine than average.

options.text: More mitochondria, suggesting heavy endurance training
options.why: Carnosine tracks fibre type area, not mitochondrial content.

options.text: Nothing, since carnosine has no link with fibre type
options.why: Carnosine correlated with type II area, though the check against biopsies was small.

variants.stem: A triathlete has one thigh biopsy in spring (55% type I) and one in autumn (63% type I), with a season of training between. What is the best reading?

options.text: The change fits within single-biopsy noise, so no shift is shown
options.why: Right: one biopsy has a CV of 13–18%, and ±10 percentage points needs about three biopsies.

options.text: Training turned 8% of her fibres from type II to type I
options.why: 8 percentage points is within the sampling error of single biopsies; it may not be a real change.

options.text: Her muscle grew new type I fibres over the season
options.why: Even if the change were real, it wouldn't show new fibres; and here it may be noise.

options.text: The spring biopsy must have been taken wrongly
options.why: No error is needed: patchy fibre types make single samples differ.

variants.stem: How common are pure type IIx fibres in the thigh muscle of healthy, active young adults?

options.text: Rare: about 0.1% of fibres on average
options.why: Right: most samples had none; pure IIx averaged 0.1% of fibres.

options.text: About a quarter of all fibres
options.why: 24% IIx was found in one champion sprinter, an exception.

options.text: About half of all fibres
options.why: That is closer to the type I share in many people.

options.text: Absent, since humans have no IIx myosin
options.why: Humans do have MHC IIx; it is just rare in active muscle.

variants.stem: In 19 trained cyclists, % type I fibres correlated with cycling efficiency (r = 0.85). What limits the claim that having more type I fibres makes a cyclist more efficient?

options.text: It measured each rider once, so it shows a link, not cause
options.why: Right: a cross-sectional link can't show which comes first, or rule out a third factor such as years of training.

options.text: r = 0.85 is too weak to mean anything
options.why: 0.85 is a strong correlation; the problem is the design, not the size.

options.text: Efficiency can't be measured on a cycle ergometer
options.why: Gross and delta efficiency are routinely measured on ergometers from VO₂ and RER.

options.text: Type I fibres are found only in runners, not cyclists
options.why: Cyclists' thighs had 32–76% type I fibres in this very study.
